performers: Sviatoslav Richter; Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra; Stanisław Wisłocki
question: What changes when the quiet second theme becomes the finale’s main arrival?
intro: A quick first theme and a broad second theme trade places between piano and orchestra. The longer melody returns in different keys before reaching C major near the end; follow how its accompaniment and orchestral weight change with each return.

cues.title: The orchestra prepares the soloist
cues.text: The finale begins quietly, before the piano takes over. Short string figures and a lightly marked bass supply motion without yet giving the music the weight of the later tutti passages.
cues.evidence: Full score pp. 68–69 shows the piano resting beneath quiet strings, clarinets, bassoons and tuba. The analysis places very low level in the opening ten seconds, followed by a strong rise around 0:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Short figures, quick responses
cues.text: In the first thematic group, follow the piano’s short rhythmic shapes rather than only its runs. The orchestra often replies in brief gestures, making room for the soloist’s more continuous motion.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 70–75 gives the piano’s first-theme writing with short wind and string responses. A boundary at 0:30 follows the introductory crescendo; the placement identifies a broad first-theme region, not a particular reply.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Richter in Warsaw
cues.text: This performance pairs Sviatoslav Richter with the Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra under Stanisław Wisłocki. Recorded in 1959 for Deutsche Grammophon, it belongs to the same recording as the preceding two movements on this site.
cues.evidence: The selected Commons file identifies performers, year and Deutsche Grammophon. Pianist Discography lists the concerto under DG 138 076: https://pianistdiscography.com/discography/pianistLabel.php?cdnum=2186
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A broad melody in the orchestra
cues.text: The second theme slows the rate of melodic movement. Its first presentation belongs to oboe and violas, with the piano resting; listen for a long phrase replacing the earlier exchange of short figures.
cues.evidence: Score p. 77 marks Moderato and gives the B♭-major melody to solo oboe and violas. The report shows a substantial level and onset-density reduction around 1:40–1:55, supporting an approximate second-theme region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano takes up the line
cues.text: When the piano carries the broad melody, distinguish its singing upper line from the broken chords beneath it. The soloist can be both melody and accompaniment; an orchestral concerto need not divide those jobs permanently.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 78–79 gives the second theme to piano above its own arpeggiated accompaniment, with restrained orchestral support. The analysis’s gradual increase in activity after 2:15 supports broad placement, not the exact handover.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A swell inside the long theme
cues.text: The lyrical group has its own accumulation and retreat. Listen across the swell as one extended phrase, rather than treating the louder passage as a new theme each time the sound grows.
cues.evidence: Level rises from approximately −24 dB at 2:20 to −13.5 at 2:55, then drops to −33.1 at 3:10. This supports a broad rise and withdrawal without identifying a particular orchestral cause.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Dahl and the new concerto
cues.text: Rachmaninoff received treatment from Nikolai Dahl in early 1900 after a prolonged loss of confidence in composing. The Second Concerto emerged during his return to sustained composition; its dedication names Dahl.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note describes treatment from January to April 1900 and the concerto’s dedication: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The short material regains force
cues.text: After the lyrical group’s withdrawal, a much stronger passage restores sharply articulated motion. Keep the first theme’s smaller rhythmic shapes in mind as the music begins to develop and redistribute them.
cues.evidence: The score’s central development restores active first-group material. Boundaries at 3:52 and 3:58 precede a level jump from −24.1 dB at 3:55 to −7 at 4:00; this locates a broad developmental change.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Development need not stay loud
cues.text: The central stretch soon falls back in volume. Follow the continuing figures through that quieter passage: development can work by isolating and repeating a small shape, not only by making the whole orchestra louder.
cues.evidence: Following the 4:00–4:10 crest, level falls to −31.2 dB at 4:35 and remains markedly lower around 4:40–4:50. The listening invitation concerns continuity of short figures, not an unverified instrument entrance.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A longer accumulation
cues.text: The central music gathers intensity again over a longer span. Listen for successive increases rather than a single sudden leap: repeating fragments can build pressure while their harmonic setting keeps moving.
cues.evidence: The analysis rises from roughly −22.6 dB at 5:00 to −9 at 5:25, with another crest near 5:55. The report’s changing key estimates support instability only; no exact chord progression is inferred from them.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The finale was heard first
cues.text: Rachmaninoff performed the concerto’s second and third movements in Moscow on 15 December 1900, with Alexander Siloti conducting. The complete three-movement concerto followed in November 1901, with the same soloist and conductor.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO programme note gives the partial premiere and complete premiere dates and personnel: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The broad theme in another key
cues.text: The second theme returns in D♭ major rather than its earlier B♭ major. Its contour remains recognisable, but the score changes its colour too: flute and first violins lead this orchestral presentation.
cues.evidence: Score p. 97 explicitly restores Moderato, with the transposed theme in flute and first violins. Boundaries at 6:04 and 6:16, lower level and D♭-region pitch estimates support the approximate return at 6:16.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognise the accompaniment as well
cues.text: As the piano continues the returning lyrical group, compare its broken-chord support with the first presentation. A familiar accompaniment can make a transposed melody feel like a return even before its whole phrase has unfolded.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 98–99 restores the piano’s lyrical line over arpeggiated accompaniment in the transposed setting. The analysis shows renewed activity and a gradual swell through about 6:45–7:25; timing is passage-level.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another withdrawal
cues.text: The returning lyrical group recedes before the final drive. Keep its long melody in memory through the quieter continuation: the finale has not yet reached the full C-major statement that will settle the theme’s tonal route.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −12.9 dB at 7:25 to −31.4 at 7:40. The score reserves the Maestoso C-major version for pp. 109–112; this note does not claim a precise harmonic event at 7:35.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A melody with another title
cues.text: The finale’s second theme later supplied the melody of the popular song Full Moon and Empty Arms. The song’s existence is a later reception history, not a programme attached to Rachmaninoff’s concerto.
cues.evidence: The BSO programme note identifies the finale’s melody as the source of Full Moon and Empty Arms: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6. No unsupported publication date or lyricist credit is added.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A quiet start to the final drive
cues.text: The closing build begins below the movement’s earlier peaks. Listen for small active figures gathering weight; a coda can start by withholding the full orchestral sound rather than announcing the ending at once.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 103–108 develops active material towards the final Presto and piano flourish. Analysis boundaries cluster at 8:20–8:40 while level remains low, before a sustained increase from about 8:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The pressure accumulates
cues.text: The later build reaches a stronger level and keeps renewing its momentum. Listen across the local rises and falls towards the larger arrival still ahead, rather than mistaking the first loud crest for the final theme.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −28.5 dB at 8:50 to −9.6 at 9:10, then reaches a further sustained crest around 9:45–9:55. This describes the measured build without equating loudness with tempo.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A flourish before the broadening
cues.text: Before the final broad statement, the score gives the piano a freer sweep while the orchestra pauses. Listen for the contrast between fast surface motion and the slower, chordal weight of the theme that follows.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 108–109 contains Presto, an orchestral fermata and the solo flourish leading to Maestoso. Boundaries at 10:00 and 10:16 frame the approach; the exact start of the flourish is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The long theme reaches C major
cues.text: The second theme now arrives in C major with much greater orchestral weight. Its long notes stand above the piano’s chordal activity: the melody heard quietly earlier has become the movement’s largest shared statement.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 109–112 gives Maestoso in C major to the expanded orchestra with chordal piano writing. The strongest analysis boundary is 10:16; C-major pitch content and sustained high level follow it.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From broad theme to quick close
cues.text: After the broadened melody, Più vivo releases the piano into quicker closing figures. The ending does not introduce another lyrical subject: rapid motion and repeated orchestral chords bring the C-major conclusion into focus.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 112–116 marks Più vivo and gives rapid piano figures with orchestral chordal punctuation. The report shows high onset activity near 11:05–11:25 and its loudest five-second window at 11:20; exact tempo-change timing is estimated.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After the last chords
cues.text: Let the recorded decay complete the ending. The final attacks have already supplied the close; the remaining sound is the hall and instruments falling quiet, not the beginning of another phrase.
cues.evidence: Level drops from −5.2 dB at 11:25 to −33.2 at 11:30 and −73.2 at 11:35. The file ends at 11:39.7; the note describes the decay rather than assigning a precise final release.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

transitions.title: The orchestra launches the piano’s quick figures
transitions.how: The short orchestral introduction grows from quiet string figures into a fuller crescendo. The piano answers with a sweeping passage and then establishes the first group’s active rhythmic profile. As the solo line takes over, the orchestral texture becomes more intermittent: brief wind replies and plucked string support leave the piano room to define the theme.
transitions.evidence: Full score pp. 68–72 supplies the introductory crescendo, solo sweep and changing accompaniment. The analysis’s rise at 0:15 and boundary at 0:30 locate a broad handover, not a checked first-theme onset.

transitions.title: The piano yields to a longer melody
transitions.how: The quick piano writing broadens through a ritardando. At Moderato, the soloist rests and oboe and violas begin the long second theme in B♭ major, supported by quiet horn harmony and lower strings. This join changes the phrase scale as well as the scoring: held notes replace the first group’s short exchanges, and the orchestra introduces the melody before the piano takes it up.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 77 shows ritardando, Moderato, B♭-major theme, oboe/viola melody and resting piano. The report’s lower level and reduced onset density from about 1:40 support the approximate join.

transitions.title: Short material displaces the lyrical continuation
transitions.how: The second group’s long continuation subsides before the central working of shorter material. Renewed chordal attacks and quicker piano figures recover the active character of the first group; fragments can now be repeated against changing harmonic ground rather than completing another broad lyrical statement. The contrast is a change of thematic scale and texture, not simply a louder repetition of the second theme.
transitions.evidence: The central full-score passage, around pp. 83–85, works with active first-group material. Boundaries at 3:52 and 3:58 and a large level increase at 4:00 anchor this provisional developmental region.

transitions.title: The melody returns with new orchestral colour
transitions.how: After the active first-group recovery, the piano broadens and withdraws again. Moderato restores the second theme, but now in D♭ major with flute and first violins carrying its line. Clarinets, bassoons and the remaining strings support the phrase. Its contour links the return to the earlier B♭-major statement while both key and orchestral leadership have changed.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 96–97 supplies the withdrawal and D♭-major Moderato, led by flute and first violins. The 6:16 boundary, reduced onset density and D♭-region estimate corroborate broad placement.

transitions.title: The lyrical group gives way to fragments
transitions.how: The returning lyrical group recedes and the music turns back towards shorter, more active figures. Instead of providing the final tonic statement immediately, Rachmaninoff starts the closing drive at a restrained level and accumulates momentum through repeated patterns and thicker piano writing. The long melody is withheld until after the later Presto and solo flourish.
transitions.evidence: The full score’s closing preparation, pp. 103–108, leads through active figures to Presto and the flourish. Analysis boundaries at 8:20, 8:28 and 8:36 locate a quieter turning region before the build after 8:55.

transitions.title: A solo flourish opens the major-key arrival
transitions.how: The Presto drive reaches a held orchestral point, allowing the piano a free flourish. A fermata separates this quick motion from Maestoso: the second theme arrives in C major, broadened across winds and strings, with brass support and chordal piano writing beneath it. The join resolves the melody’s tonal route while transforming the small-scale first statement into a shared orchestral arrival.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 108–110 supplies the Presto, fermata, solo flourish and Maestoso C-major return. The report’s strongest boundary at 10:16 and high C-major region thereafter support the estimated culmination.

source.title: Rachmaninoff, Piano Concerto No. 2, full score, Gutheil engraving in Boosey & Hawkes reprint, plate B. & H. 16674
source.locator: Finale, printed pp. 68–116 (PDF pp. 66–114). Representative passage-level scoring; approximate times follow measured contrasts at 0:30, 1:40, 3:58, 6:16, 8:28 and 10:16, not bar alignment or exact entrances.

timeline.note: Quiet introductory string figures with clarinet, bassoon and tuba support; the piano rests (pp. 68–69).
The introductory crescendo leads into the solo sweep; orchestral chords frame the moving piano line (pp. 69–70, approximate).
First-group piano writing with brief upper-wind replies and plucked string support (pp. 71–72).
The first group expands through exchanges with reeds, horns and strings; this is a passage summary, not a simultaneous attack (pp. 73–75).
At the first Moderato, oboe and violas carry the broad theme while the piano rests; horn harmony and lower strings support them (p. 77).
The piano takes the lyrical line above its own broken chords, with restrained reed and string support (pp. 78–79, approximate).
Active central piano writing is punctuated by orchestral chords and timpani; instrumentation describes the surrounding development rather than every instant (around p. 84).
Piano figures and chordal statements gather support from winds, brass and strings through the later central accumulation (pp. 91–93, approximate).
The transposed second theme belongs to flute and first violins; clarinets, bassoons and the remaining strings support it while piano rests (p. 97).
Piano resumes the lyrical continuation in D♭ major, with sustained reed and string parts (pp. 98–99, approximate).
The Presto drive uses the full ensemble before the held point and piano flourish (p. 108; time approximate).
The piano’s freer flourish occupies the gap before Maestoso; the orchestra pauses around its held chord (pp. 108–109, approximate).
The Maestoso theme broadens across winds and strings above chordal piano writing, horns and lower brass; trumpets, bass drum and cymbals rest (pp. 109–110).
Più vivo and the final bars combine quick piano motion with repeated full-orchestra chords, including timpani, bass drum and cymbals (pp. 112–116).

composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
facts: Moscow Conservatory: piano with Nikolai Zverev and Alexander Siloti; counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev, composition with Anton Arensky

Ivanovka near Tambov · Dresden · New York · Villa Senar, Lake Lucerne · Beverly Hills

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
